Broadway Theatre. Professional theatrical productions staged on the main commercial stages of the Theatre District in midtown New York City. Encompassing drama, comedy, musicals, and experimental work, Broadway is the premier commercial theater venue in the United States and a major force in global popular culture.

The term Broadway derives from the historic avenue in New York. The district emerged as a theatrical center in the early twentieth century and solidified as America's theatrical capital. It distinguishes itself from Off-Broadway, which features smaller, less commercial venues, and Off-Off-Broadway, which is experimental and non-commercial.

The Broadway musical became a distinctive American form, combining popular music, theatrical storytelling, choreography, and visual spectacle. Early musicals drew on vaudeville, operetta, and revue traditions. Show Boat in nineteen twenty-seven and Oklahoma in nineteen forty-three established the modern integrated musical. Iconic composers like Richard Rodgers, George Gershwin, Leonard Bernstein, and Stephen Sondheim created works that defined both theater and American popular music.

Broadway reached peak cultural influence mid-twentieth century. Musicals like The Sound of Music, Funny Girl, and West Side Story dominated entertainment and won international acclaim. Contemporary Broadway encompasses revival productions, star vehicles, and serious drama alongside musicals, with major film transfers and international revivals cycling through regularly. The form pioneered by Broadway—integrated song and dance advancing plot and character development—has become the global template for musical theater.
